chunks: Al-Saffar narrated from Al-Sindi, from Muhammad ibn al-Rabi', from Yahya ibn al-Mubarak, from 'Abd Allah ibn Jabalah, from 'Asim al-Hannat, from Abi Hamzah al-Thumali, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, who said:

I said to him, “May I be made your ransom, what do you say about a man who struck another man on the head with a tent-pole, causing him to become addled — meaning that his intellect departed?” He said, “The diyah is upon him.” I said, “If he lived for ten days, or less, or more, and then his intellect returned to him, does he still have the right to take the diyah?” He said, “No; the diyah has already taken effect with all that it includes.” I said, “If he died after two or three months, and his associates said: We want to kill the man who struck him?” He said, “If they wish to kill him, they must return the diyah within the period between them and one year. Once the year has passed, they have no right to kill him, and the diyah has taken effect with all that it includes.”

key_terms.الدِّيَةُ: financial compensation due for bodily injury or killing
key_terms.السَّنَةُ: the one-year period mentioned as the limit in this ruling
key_terms.ذَهَبَ عَقْلُهُ: his intellect departed; he lost his mental faculty
key_terms.فَأَمِهَ: he became mentally impaired or lost sound understanding

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if someone loses his intellect from a head injury and later dies after diyah was paid?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a legal ruling on compensation and retaliation in a case where a head injury causes loss of intellect. It states that diyah becomes due for the injury, and if the victim later dies, the right to retaliatory killing is restricted by the prior acceptance of diyah and by a one-year limit.
